name: Longest unbroken run of serials
returns: a list of two whole numbers
brief:
A depot scans the serial numbers of returned parcels into `serials`, in any order and with repeats. A run is a block of consecutive whole numbers that are all present. Return `[first, length]` for the longest run. On a tie, return the run with the smallest first serial. Return `[0, 0]` when `serials` is empty.

Write `longest_serial_run(serials)`.

Example. For `[50, 7, 90, 5, 8, 6, 9]` the serials 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 are all present. No longer run exists, so the answer is `[5, 5]`.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ serials, each a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n)$ expected time is the target with a set. Sorting first also passes; walking up from every serial does not.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Put the serials in a set. Start counting only from a serial whose predecessor is missing, so each run is walked once.

examples.note: Serials 5 to 9 make a run of 5. 50 and 90 are runs of 1.
Two runs of length 2 tie, and the one starting at 1 starts lower.

tests.call: longest_serial_run([10 ** 9 - i for i in range(100000)] + [-10 ** 9 + i for i in range(100000)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: A run is counted only from its lowest serial, the one whose predecessor is missing.
Repeats must not lengthen a run, and a tie goes to the lower first serial.
Each serial is stepped over at most twice, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It sorts but lets a repeated serial lengthen the run, so `[1, 2, 2, 3]` counts four.
It replaces the best run on a tie, so the run with the larger first serial wins.
It walks up from every serial, not just from run starts, which is $O(n^2)$ on one long run.
Looping over the list, not the set, walks a run again for every repeat of its first serial.
